predictions.instrument: paired element-level marks from two assessors on a subset of defences, with agreement computed separately for the overall result and for the per-element pattern. **This is the direct test of §8's third objection**, and a confirmation means the single-assessor arrangement is producing a defensible outcome by an undocumented route — which is the condition the literature warns about and the one this occasion cannot currently detect.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Candidates who name a mistake of their own in the defence will score no differently on other elements than those who do not.
predictions.instrument: element-level marks paired against the presence of a self-attributed failure. **The design expects this prediction to hold**, and if it fails — if self-attribution correlates with lower marks — the reattribution warning sign is punishing honesty and must be removed.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most learners will put descriptive text on diagram edges at first attempt, before the integers-only rule is enforced.
predictions.instrument: the first submitted diagram, coded *integers only* / *mixed* / *text* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Inferred-values sections will record fewer inferences than a second reader can identify from the same source documents.
predictions.instrument: independent re-derivation of the attribute table by a second reader working from the same inputs, compared row by row against the learner's provenance section. **This predicts the failure of the session's central countermeasure**, and it is included because a control whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption. If it holds, the provenance side-channel is honest in intent and lossy in fact, and [S054](/wiki/seminars/S054.md) is teaching against a defect the cohort has already committed.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who attribute one flow completely before starting others will revise their closed classification list; those who attribute in parallel will not.
predictions.instrument: the list's revision record against the recorded attribution order.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Learners who hand the whole table to an agent will submit shorter open-questions lists than those who attributed a flow by hand first.
predictions.instrument: the open-questions list against the recorded working method, paired per learner. **If this fails, the workflow's ordering has no support and should be rewritten as a preference rather than a sequence.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: In exercise 4, the fed agent run will declare fewer inferences in `inferred.yaml` than the starved run, while filling more cells.
predictions.instrument: the two generated files, compared on filled-cell count and declared-inference count. **This is the session's only direct test of the claim that more context suppresses declared uncertainty**, and a null result would mean the information-diet argument in §3.10 is asserted rather than demonstrated.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-1 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will produce joinable flow identifiers more often than learners who read the same criterion without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: the submitted `dataflows.yaml`, coded for identifier stability by a second reader, across two cohorts — or, absent two cohorts, a within-cohort split on whether exercise 3 was completed. **This is the session's only direct test of the mechanism §3.2 rests on.**

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: A majority of learners will find at least one component in the machine-generated inventory that is absent from their hand-built one, and a minority will record anything that neither could see.
predictions.instrument: the two inventories plus `open-questions.md`, coded for entries of the third kind. **The second half is the interesting half**, and if it comes out near zero the exercise is teaching inventory rather than teaching the limits of inventory.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most exclusion registers will list incidents rather than categories at first attempt.
predictions.instrument: the submitted register, coded *categorical* / *mixed* / *incident list* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Learners will discard fewer candidates than a second reader applying the same binding rule to the same candidate list.
predictions.instrument: independent application of the rule by a second reader, compared against the learner's discard log.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Reviewers given only the discard log will identify a wrongly discarded threat for most learners.
predictions.instrument: exercise 2's written outcome, recorded per learner as *found* / *not found*.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Learners who record their candidate source and its currency will revise their registry after the adversarial second agent; those who do not will not.
predictions.instrument: the registry's revision record against the presence of a dated source statement, paired per learner. **If this fails, the dated-source requirement is disclosure with no behavioural effect and should be stated as such rather than taught as a countermeasure.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: In exercise 5, a substantial proportion of the items learners initially transcribe from machine-generated posture output will be recommendations rather than threats — imperatives with no component and no flow.
predictions.instrument: the learner's own two counts, audited by a second reader against the submitted registry.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-3 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will place unbindable threats in the exclusion register more often, and force-bind them into the registry less often, than learners who read the same criterion without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: the registry and register together, coded for force-binding by a second reader, across two cohorts — or, absent two cohorts, a within-cohort split on whether exercise 3 was completed. **This is the session's only direct test of the mechanism §3.2 rests on.**

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Exclusion registers will be read by nobody except the assessor.
predictions.instrument: access or citation of the register in any downstream artefact — [S053](/wiki/seminars/S053.md)'s mapping, [S055](/wiki/seminars/S055.md)'s plan defence — counted per learner. **This predicts the failure of the session's own central countermeasure**, and it is included because §8's first objection is that the register creates a tidier artefact with the same fate as the log. If it holds, the register's value is confined to the act of writing it, and the paper should say so rather than claiming a reader it does not have.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most first mappings will credit at least one control against threats spanning unrelated mechanisms without a per-attachment defence.
predictions.instrument: the submitted mapping, with each control's attachments coded *defended individually* / *undefended* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Reviewers applying the four tests will find a wrong-layer, wrong-direction or wrong-surface credit in most mappings.
predictions.instrument: exercise 4's written outcome, recorded per learner as *found* / *not found*, with the test that caught it.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Declared switch points will be inconsistent with the learner's own mapping behaviour.
predictions.instrument: the declared switch against the breadth of the submitted mapping, coded *consistent* / *inconsistent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Mapping reasons produced from full entries will restate the entries more often than mapping reasons produced from compact indexes.
predictions.instrument: reasons coded *mechanism* / *restatement*, compared across learners by recorded working method. **If this fails, the information-diet claim carried from [S051](/wiki/seminars/S051.md) has no support at this scale and the compact index should be taught as an efficiency rather than as a quality measure.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: In exercise 1, learners will classify a substantial share of their own controls as *governance* or *monitoring* when forced to choose one word, and the share will be higher for controls they did not personally deploy.
predictions.instrument: the learner's own count, audited by a second reader, split by whether the learner deployed the control.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: For most learners, at least one posture surface will have an owner they cannot name at the start of the session and can name at the end.
predictions.instrument: the control inventory's owner fields, compared against a pre-session written attempt at the same list. **If this fails — if learners can already name both owners — the surface test is teaching an organisational fact the cohort already holds**, and its value is confined to the layer, direction and plane tests it accompanies.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Every submitted three-way accounting will reconcile, and reconciliation will not correlate with any second reader's judgement of mapping quality.
predictions.instrument: the reconciliation outcome against an independent quality rating of the same mappings. **This predicts the failure of an assessed property of this session**, and it is included because §8's fourth objection concedes that arithmetic is satisfiable by a drawer. If it holds, the reconciliation should be retained as a hygiene check and removed from anything that reads as a quality signal.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-1 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will produce negative control claims naming a test more often than learners who read the same criterion without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: the submitted mapping's unmapped-control rationales, coded *names a test* / *hedges* by a second reader, across two cohorts — or, absent two cohorts, a within-cohort split on completion of exercise 3.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most learners will be unable to name a step at which the asker's identity is compared against a document's permissions, and will instead describe a filter their application constructs.
predictions.instrument: the written answer to opening item 1, coded *names a check* / *names a filter* / *names nothing* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: In the two-persona exercise, the unauthorised persona will receive the substance of a restricted document for most learners at first attempt.
predictions.instrument: the two transcripts, with the restricted content's presence in the unauthorised answer judged by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Most learners will answer opening item 4 — where do the permissions live once documents are chunked — from assumption rather than from inspection, and will be wrong.
predictions.instrument: the written answer against the evidence field in the submitted chunk-projection statement.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: A substantial proportion of measured revocation windows will exceed the duration of the session, so the learner records *still retrievable when I stopped* rather than an elapsed time.
predictions.instrument: the revocation-window statements, coded *measured* / *exceeded session* / *not attempted*. **If almost every window is short, the session over-weights this failure and should say so.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Most first traces will describe a tendency rather than name a step.
predictions.instrument: the submitted trace, coded *step-level* / *stage-level* / *tendency* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Most learners will identify marker loss and not optimistic resolution.
predictions.instrument: the two-defect statement, coded for which defects appear, recorded per learner.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners whose [S051](/wiki/seminars/S051.md) provenance section was empty will report identical double scores and will conclude their artefact is sound rather than that their marking failed.
predictions.instrument: the two scores paired with the learner's stated conclusion, against the provenance section's content.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Proposed smallest changes will be process additions more often than artefact or step changes.
predictions.instrument: the proposed change, coded *artefact change* / *step change* / *process addition*. **If this holds, the affordability constraint is not doing its work and the workflow should name the permitted classes of change rather than describing them.**

predictions.label: Prediction 9.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-1 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will produce authorisation traces containing a `none` row more often than learners who read the same criterion without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: the submitted trace, coded for the presence of an honestly-marked uncompared step, across two cohorts — or, absent two cohorts, a within-cohort split on completion of exercise 3. **This is the session's only direct test of the mechanism §3.2 rests on.**

predictions.label: Prediction 10.
predictions.claim: In exercise 7, a majority of learners will find at least one self-verification checklist in their own artefacts, and a minority will find one rendered into a deliverable with its ticks intact.
predictions.instrument: the classification submitted, audited by a second reader against the learner's artefacts. **This predicts the failure of the session's own final countermeasure**: if the minority is near zero, the audit-trail costume is a defect of the specimen rather than a habit the cohort has, and the exercise should be re-scoped to reading rather than self-inspection.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will shorten the unmitigated list between their answer to opening item 2 and the submitted plan.
predictions.instrument: the submitted opening answers against the plan's contents, compared per candidate by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will accept the assessor's offered improvement.
predictions.instrument: the defence recorded as *accepted* / *declined*, with the evidential threshold named where declined.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Named closure blind spots will be restatements of the criterion more often than specific undetectable fixes.
predictions.instrument: each blind spot coded *specific fix* / *restatement* / *absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: An agent asked to score a submitted plan favourably will do so without regard to whether any mitigation is implemented.
predictions.instrument: the agent's assessment against the plan's own status column, paired per candidate. **If this fails — if the agent's assessment tracks implementation — the session's claim that such rubrics are satisfiable by naming has no support at this scale and the workflow's final step should be removed.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will describe their single control verification as though it established a general property, until prompted.
predictions.instrument: the submitted plan's verification language, coded *conditions stated* / *unconditioned* by a second reader, before and after exercise 3's prompt.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: A minority of candidates will notice that several of their controls were configured together and verified together, and are therefore closer to one observation than to several.
predictions.instrument: the plan's verification section, coded for whether the grouping is acknowledged. **This is the weakest link in the occasion's statistical argument** and if the minority is very small the transfer in §3.6 is too abstract to teach in this position and should move to a measurement session.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Candidates whose plans state that no approval point exists will outnumber those who name one, and a minority of those who name one will name a person who reads nothing.
predictions.instrument: the submitted plans, coded *absence stated* / *substantive gate* / *nominal gate* by a second reader who is permitted to ask the candidate what the approver reads.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Candidates instructed to compare their item-2 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 4) will retain more of their own uncomfortable material in the submitted plan than candidates who read the same criterion without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: the opening answer against the plan, coded for retention, across two cohorts — or, absent two cohorts, a within-cohort split on completion of exercise 4. **This is the occasion's only direct test of the mechanism its opening rests on.**

predictions.label: Prediction 9.
predictions.claim: The elements a second assessor disagrees on will cluster on 3, 9 and 11 — generic mitigation, closure blind spot, and adversarial input — rather than on the structural elements.
predictions.instrument: double-marking of a sample, with disagreements recorded by element. **This predicts the failure of the specification's own claim to be checkable without domain expertise**, and if it holds those three elements need either a worked reference or removal, because an element two assessors read differently is a marker's opinion in a specification's clothing — which is the fault [S054](/wiki/seminars/S054.md) teaches candidates to detect.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most first alternatives will describe the current process rather than a from-scratch design.
predictions.instrument: the submitted alternative, coded *designed* / *partially designed* / *status quo* by a second reader, using the presence of components, an operator and a named failure mode.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most disconfirming-evidence statements will name evidence available only after commitment.
predictions.instrument: each statement coded *available during the engagement* / *available only afterwards* / *absent*.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Cost comparisons will price the non-AI alternative more completely than the option being built, and the `causation_owner` field will be the most frequently empty field in the record.
predictions.instrument: a category-by-category presence check across both columns by a second reader, using the named categories, plus a completeness count per field across the cohort.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Despite the stated-detectability field, a majority of records will report a comparative conclusion without stating what difference the comparison could have detected, or will state it as *unknown* and then draw a confident conclusion anyway.
predictions.instrument: the records, coded for whether the detectability statement and the conclusion are consistent. **This predicts the failure of §5's newest countermeasure**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Learners whose systems are retrieval problems will produce substantially more complete alternatives than learners whose systems are open-ended generation problems, and the gap will not be visible in the assessed elements.
predictions.instrument: submissions stratified by problem type and coded on the same *designed / partially designed / status quo* scale. **This is the instrument attached to §8's third objection**, and a confirmation means the session is exempting the teams whose systems infer most.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: A minority of learners will attempt to build the deterministic alternative at all, and among those who do, a majority will report being surprised by how well it performed on their own frozen set.
predictions.instrument: a built/not-built count, plus a pre-recorded expectation compared against the observed result per learner. **If the surprise does not occur, the session's central empirical wager is wrong for this cohort's problem set**, and the material's use of the retrieval evidence should be demoted from argument to illustration.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most first tests will be effort tests in new wording.
predictions.instrument: the submitted test, with a second reader determining whether its answer varies with the amount of work done.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Independent classification will disagree on at least one deliverable for most learners.
predictions.instrument: the paired classifications from the review exercise, compared item by item.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: A majority of classifications will record the initiation model for the obvious agent deliverables and omit it for the non-agent ones — the harness, the prompt file, the exported configuration.
predictions.instrument: per-deliverable field completeness, stratified by deliverable type. **This predicts the partial failure of §5's initiation-model countermeasure**, and the omission matters because a scheduled trigger is usually attached to the unglamorous artefact rather than to the one everybody is watching.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: The one-setting-away field will be the least completed field in the artefact, and where completed will under-count.
predictions.instrument: completeness per field across the cohort, plus a second reader independently enumerating the settings for a sample and comparing counts.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Wrongly included cases will be absent more often than wrongly excluded cases.
predictions.instrument: the presence of each named case, coded per learner. **If this fails, the over-inclusion cost is more salient to learners than the design expects and §3.9's symmetry argument needs revisiting.**

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners will classify orchestrator ownership less accurately after this session than a cohort taught the five axes with equal weight.
predictions.instrument: a common classification task on a system none of the cohort built, marked for accuracy per axis, across two cohorts taught differently — or, absent two cohorts, per-axis accuracy compared against the axis the session emphasised. **This is the instrument attached to §8's third objection**, and a confirmation means the design bought its emphasis at a measurable cost.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: The set of deliverables a reviewer would be uncomfortable owning will differ from the learner's in-scope set.
predictions.instrument: the two sets compared per learner, with the difference recorded in both directions.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Most learners will name at least one control in their test that can only observe after the fact, and will not have noticed.
predictions.instrument: each control named in the submitted test, coded *preventive* / *detective* by a second reader against the control's documented mechanism, compared with whether the learner's own artefact records the distinction anywhere. **A null result — learners spontaneously distinguishing enforcement from notification — would mean §3's latency material is redundant** and it should be cut to a single line in the workflow rather than kept as a subsection.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most triggers will be calendar-based or person-dependent rather than bound to a state change.
predictions.instrument: the submitted trigger, coded *state change with actor* / *calendar* / *person* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most falsifiable rewrites will supply a measurement and an owner while omitting a threshold or a verification method.
predictions.instrument: a four-field presence check on each rewritten claim.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Version fields will contain a single entry at submission.
predictions.instrument: the revision history's entry count at the point of submission.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Learners will judge that their review will be paid more often than an independent reader given the same price judges it will.
predictions.instrument: the learner's stated judgement against a second reader's, paired per learner. **If this fails, learners are already realistic about review capacity and the pricing element is confirming rather than teaching.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of resolution blocks will state a scope, a cadence and a latency, and a majority of *outside all three* entries will be empty or generic.
predictions.instrument: per-field completeness, with the *outside all three* entries coded *specific to this system* / *generic* / *absent* by a second reader. **This predicts the failure of §5's newest countermeasure and is the instrument attached to §8's third objection**, and a confirmation means the resolution block is producing plausible fiction rather than characterisation.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: When learners date their own harm-register entries, a substantial share will be dated after the point at which the assessment was formally due.
predictions.instrument: the dated register from exercise 4, with entries coded *specifiable in advance* / *output-dependent* by a second reader. **If instead almost all entries are pre-datable, §3.5's criteria-drift argument does not apply to this artefact class** and §8's fourth objection resolves in the opposite direction from the one this paper expects.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners will resist the expiry element more than any other, and will set expiry conditions that cannot be evaluated without the author present.
predictions.instrument: the expiry conditions, coded *evaluable by a stranger* / *requires the author* / *absent*, alongside a short free-text objection collected at the point the element is set.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most records will name a function rather than a person, or a body with a chair and papers.
predictions.instrument: the submitted record, coded *named person* / *named body with chair and papers* / *function* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most deviations will lack an expiry at first attempt.
predictions.instrument: a presence check for expiry and revisit condition on each deviation submitted.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Most dodge checks will be answered in the negative.
predictions.instrument: the learner's answer, paired with a second reader's independent attempt to construct a narrower description of the same system that avoids the classification.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Sensitive uses will be located inside the system more often than in the human process around it.
predictions.instrument: the location coded against the categories in the learner's [S052](/wiki/seminars/S052.md) exclusion register. **If this holds, the module's claim that the exclusion register is the right input here is not being realised in practice, and the workflow's ordering should be reconsidered.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Where a decision-maker is named, a substantial share will turn out to have been asked for an authorisation rather than for an opinion.
predictions.instrument: the named decision-maker interviewed, or the record's *what they saw* field coded *judgement artefact* / *access request* / *unclear* by a second reader. **This is the instrument for §5's newest countermeasure**, and a confirmation means the session is recording approvals and calling them decisions.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Cohort determinations will cluster around review, approval and eligibility workflows — the domain of the single recorded refusal — and under-represent sensitive uses in monitoring, prioritisation and resource allocation.
predictions.instrument: determinations coded by domain and compared against the domain distribution of the cohort's actual systems. **This is the instrument attached to §8's second objection**, and a confirmation means the single case is functioning as a template for what counts rather than for how to write it.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners will spend more time on the inventory and diff than on the determination and its reasoning, and the reasoning field will be the shortest substantive field in most records.
predictions.instrument: self-reported time allocation, plus field-length and substantiation quality coded by a second reader. **This predicts the failure §8's fourth objection describes**, and a confirmation means the anchor should move later in the session rather than being removed.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Learners asked to price their own refusal will describe a cost and then decline to state whether they would pay it.
predictions.instrument: the priced-refusal exercise, coded *cost stated and decision stated* / *cost stated only* / *neither*. **If the second category dominates, the exercise is producing awareness without decision**, which is the pattern the psychological-safety literature predicts and which the session has no countermeasure for.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will name nobody in answer to opening item 2 before instruction.
predictions.instrument: the submitted opening answers, coded *named person with named change* / *named person only* / *nobody* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most assessments will contain no finding reclassified as a legitimate engineering trade-off.
predictions.instrument: a presence check for a reclassification or a defended absence, recorded per candidate.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will accept the assessor's offered sign-off.
predictions.instrument: the defence recorded as *accepted* / *declined*, with the condition named where declined.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Withheld tails will be recorded without a delivery date.
predictions.instrument: a presence check for a date on the withheld set. **If this holds, the withholding requirement is producing concealment rather than sequencing and the element should be rewritten to lead with the date.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A substantial minority of bound evaluations will be green at submission, and the candidates concerned will report having chosen the concern after writing the check rather than before.
predictions.instrument: the submitted result, plus a single ordering question asked at the defence. **This predicts the failure of §5's newest countermeasure.**

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Threshold justifications will be generic — a sentence that would justify any threshold equally well — more often than they are specific to the concern.
predictions.instrument: the justifications coded *specific to this concern* / *generic* / *absent* by a second reader. **This is the instrument attached to §8's third objection**, and a confirmation means the declaration element is producing compliance rather than reasoning.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Almost no candidate will validate a judged evaluator against hand labels, and most will bind their concern to a judged evaluator rather than to a deterministic one.
predictions.instrument: the binding coded *deterministic* / *judged and validated* / *judged and unvalidated*. **If judged-and-unvalidated dominates, the occasion is teaching candidates to relocate the trust problem while believing they have solved it**, and the specification should require the deterministic tier by default.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Candidates will be unable to answer at least one of the three what-if questions with a counterfactual, answering instead by restating what they did.
predictions.instrument: the defence transcript, with each what-if answer coded *counterfactual* / *restatement* / *unanswered*. **This is the direct test of whether the borrowed discussion form is producing the evidence §3.10 claims for it**, and a null result means the occasion is a walkthrough with a better name.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most learners will be unable to answer opening item 2 before instruction.
predictions.instrument: the submitted opening answers, coded *specific signals named* / *general acknowledgement* / *absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Deletion lists will be shorter than review lists.
predictions.instrument: a count of entries on each, per learner, recorded without comparison to any target.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners will name the decision a panel changes more readily than they will name what would be lost if a kept signal stopped.
predictions.instrument: the closing exercise, recorded as *answered* / *not answered* for each of the two questions.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Most question columns will have been written against signals that already existed rather than derived independently.
predictions.instrument: a second reader comparing the question set with the pre-session signal inventory, coded *derived* / *retrofitted* / *cannot tell*. **This predicts the failure of the session's principal countermeasure** — the ordering of the workflow — and if retrofitting dominates, the session should require the question table to be submitted before the estate is examined at all.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Privacy lines will be the most frequently omitted or thinnest part of the submitted specification, and thinner than the correlation statement.
predictions.instrument: the submitted artefacts, with each of the six required parts coded *complete* / *present but generic* / *absent*. **This is the design's own test of whether stating a documentation silence is enough to make learners act on it**, and a confirmation means the silence must be converted into a required prompt rather than a warning.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners will treat a trace as a complete record of what the agent did, and will report a coverage claim — for a trace or for a query across the agent inventory — that no published figure supports, in at least one platform claim in the [S065](/wiki/seminars/S065.md) defence.
predictions.instrument: the defence transcript, coded for coverage claims made, qualified or absent, and separately for pinned versus unpinned platform claims. **This prediction was re-pointed when §3.9's gap closed.** It formerly instrumented the citation gap; it now instruments the completeness assumption, which is the failure the closed gap makes *more* likely rather than less — a learner who can walk a documented span tree has every reason to believe it is exhaustive, and nothing in the documentation tells them it is not. **A confirmation means the completeness silence must be converted into a required field on the register rather than a warning in the material.**

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners who ran the agent against their own register will delete or relocate more signals than those who used it to enumerate.
predictions.instrument: the recorded rejections against the deletion and review list lengths, per learner. **If this fails, the session's use of the agent as an adversary rather than an assistant has no support at this scale**, and the step should be rewritten as an assertion rather than presented as a demonstration.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most learners will be unable to name a real invisible fix in answer to opening item 3 before instruction.
predictions.instrument: the submitted opening answers, coded *specific fix named* / *category named* / *absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most invisible-fix registers will contain no entry inside the learner's own control until the closing exercise's second pass.
predictions.instrument: the register recorded before and after that exercise, with entries classified *within control* / *outside control*.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Most schedules will name a cadence rather than a trigger and a team rather than a person.
predictions.instrument: the schedule field, coded *state-change trigger with named person* / *cadence with named person* / *neither*.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Learners will accept at least one citation that resolves to a comment, a disabled block or an unreferenced file.
predictions.instrument: a second reader following a sample of citations per learner and recording resolution type. **If this holds, the standard's failed-search clause is not operative and the session should require citations to be resolved by somebody other than their author before submission.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of behavioural closure records will report an absence of failures without a precision line, or with a precision line written after the verdict rather than before.
predictions.instrument: the closure records, coded *precision stated before interpretation* / *stated after* / *absent*, with the ordering established from the artefact's own revision history where available. **This predicts the failure of §5's most important countermeasure**, and it is the prediction this paper most expects to be confirmed.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners who score the same stored traces under two split strategies will report surprise at the divergence, and will subsequently state their split in the closure record more often than those who did not run the exercise.
predictions.instrument: the closure records coded for a stated split, split by whether exercise 2 was completed. **If the difference is absent, the demonstration is not doing the work §4.5 claims for it** and the material should assert the point rather than stage it.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Closure records will pin the application version far more often than they pin the judge.
predictions.instrument: the records, coded for the presence of an application pin and a judge pin independently. **A large asymmetry means the rule that an evaluation pipeline must be more stable than its application has been read as a claim about the application.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most learners' first answer to opening item 1 will describe an intended quality rather than a customer floor.
predictions.instrument: the submitted opening answers, coded *customer floor* / *team intention* / *cannot tell* by a second reader, before any instruction.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Deletion records will more often name the alert removed than name what will now be missed.
predictions.instrument: per-entry presence check for the missed-event clause.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Where the interview step is run, the receiving engineer will mark alerts the learner expected to be read.
predictions.instrument: the learner's pre-interview prediction of which alerts are ignored, compared with the engineer's marking.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Unconsumed-signal registers will contain fewer entries before a second reader examines them than after.
predictions.instrument: entry count recorded at both points. **If the counts are equal, either the register is being written well or the second reader is not being given enough of the system to find anything — and the session cannot currently distinguish those, which is a defect in the instrument rather than in the prediction.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Despite the prohibition, a majority of submitted artefacts will contain at least one sentence asserting that no incident occurred, or reporting a period as clean, without naming an instrument or a resolution.
predictions.instrument: the artefacts, scanned for absolute absence claims and coded against whether the permitted form appears elsewhere in the same document. **This predicts the failure of §5's most important countermeasure and of §8's third objection's rebuttal**, and it is the prediction this paper most expects to be confirmed.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Most detection-capability statements will contain no row whose confidence in silence is recorded as *none*, on systems that run unsupervised drift detection only.
predictions.instrument: the statements, cross-checked against the learner's own description of their drift detection. **A confirmation means learners are treating the confidence column as a scale with a floor above zero**, and the material should state the *none* case as the expected outcome rather than as a permitted one.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners will be able to state scan scope, cadence and latency for the anchored posture tooling and for almost nothing else in their estate.
predictions.instrument: the resolution line, coded per instrument as *all three stated* / *partial* / *absent*, with the source of each recorded. **If this holds, the transferable lesson is the unavailability rather than the triple**, and the session should say so directly instead of implying that most vendors publish it.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Where the interview step is run, the second question — is there anything you have stopped raising — will be omitted or answered with "nothing" far more often than the first.
predictions.instrument: the interview record, coded for whether both questions were asked and what each returned. **This is the instrument attached to §3.10**, and a confirmation is consistent with either a healthy climate or an unsafe one, which is why the record must be verbatim rather than summarised.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most learners' first answer to opening item 1 will name an infrastructure unit.
predictions.instrument: the submitted opening answers, coded *customer work unit* / *infrastructure unit* / *absent* by a second reader, before instruction.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most cost models will not carry observability as a line until the third work step.
predictions.instrument: the model recorded before and after that step, with a presence check for the line.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Cost models will carry the delivery cost as a total more often than as a composition, where they carry it at all.
predictions.instrument: the delivery-cost line, coded *total or band present* / *composition disclosed* / *absent*. **This is the instrument attached to §8's first objection**, and a high absent rate would mean the narrowing conceded there has not reached the session's own text.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Where the cost-bearing decision is identified, most learners will report that cost was not a criterion when it was made.
predictions.instrument: the named decision's provenance field, coded *cost was a criterion* / *cost was not a criterion* / *cannot establish*. **If most report that cost was a criterion, either the cohort's systems are unusual or the field is being answered aspirationally, and the element should require the decision record from [S024](/wiki/seminars/S024.md) as evidence.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of first-draft models will contain a price before they contain a token path, and a substantial minority will never acquire one.
predictions.instrument: the model's revision history or, absent that, a presence check for the token-path section coded against whether each term names the decision that set it. **This predicts the failure of §5's countermeasure against the price-list model**, and it is the prediction this paper most expects to be confirmed.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: After exercise 2, learners will identify a different decision as cost-bearing than the one they named in opening item 2.
predictions.instrument: the item-2 answer against the cost-bearing decision recorded in the artefact, coded *same* / *different* / *cannot tell*. **If they are mostly the same, either the cohort's intuitions are good or the sensitivity exercise is not being run**, and the two are distinguishable only by whether the exercise's recorded output exists.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Capacity postures that record a commitment will more often assert the deploy-verify-commit order than evidence it.
predictions.instrument: the evidence field, coded *deployment identifier and date present* / *order asserted without evidence* / *order not stated*. **A large gap means the documented sequence is being repeated as a slogan**, which is the failure mode a rule inherited from documentation is most prone to.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Learners will intervene during the handover despite the prohibition.
predictions.instrument: an observer recording *intervened* / *did not intervene* per learner, with the elapsed point of intervention noted where it occurred.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will submit a readiness argument with no do-not-operate conditions, or with conditions that could not occur.
predictions.instrument: the conditions field, coded *specific and capable of firing* / *generic* / *absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most invisible-fix registers will contain no entry inside the candidate's control at first submission.
predictions.instrument: the register's entries classified *within control* / *outside control*, recorded at submission.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will accept the assessor's offered waiver.
predictions.instrument: the defence recorded as *accepted* / *declined*, with the stated reason captured where declined and coded *names what the register is load-bearing for* / *does not*.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Cost-model elements will fail most often on the customer-side date rather than on the unit or the observability line.
predictions.instrument: per-element failure counts across the cohort. **If the unit fails most often instead, [S064](/wiki/seminars/S064.md)'s opening item is not doing its work and the session should require the unit to be agreed with the customer before the model is built.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of arguments will contain at least one platform claim whose supporting silence is stated in a separate section rather than in the same sentence, or not stated at all.
predictions.instrument: the argument, coded per claim as *silence in-sentence* / *silence elsewhere in document* / *silence absent*. **This predicts the failure of §5's countermeasure against the inherited silence**, and it is the prediction this paper most expects to be confirmed.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Candidates who complete exercise 4 will name a condition sourced from a platform limit or an evaluation's precision more often than candidates who do not.
predictions.instrument: the conditions field, coded by origin and split on whether the comparison exercise was performed. **If there is no difference, the comparison step is ceremony**, and §4.4's warrant does not survive its own instrument.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Assessors' written reasons for the same candidate, where two are obtained informally, will agree on the verdict more often than on which element carried the decision.
predictions.instrument: paired written reasons on a sample, coded for verdict agreement and for element agreement independently. **This is a direct local test of the finding §3.8 borrows**, and a confirmation is an argument for the group discussion §8's third objection declines to fund.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Arguments that carry a precision line on one measurement will carry one on all of them, and arguments that omit it will omit it everywhere.
predictions.instrument: per-argument counts of measurements with and without a precision line. **A bimodal distribution means the discipline is being adopted as a habit rather than applied as a judgement**, which is the intended outcome and would be worth knowing.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will be unable to answer opening item 1 with a value and a source.
predictions.instrument: the submitted opening answers, coded *value with named source* / *value without source* / *no value* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most candidates will leave opening item 3 blank or generic before instruction, and their item 1 answers will be markedly more specific than their item 3 answers.
predictions.instrument: the answers coded *specific value capable of occurring* / *generic* / *absent*, compared across items 1 and 3 within candidate.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Where a customer is asked for a disconfirming result, most will decline to name one.
predictions.instrument: the record's customer-response field, coded *named* / *declined* / *not asked*.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Most baseline records will rest on a recollection rather than on a record made for another purpose.
predictions.instrument: the source field, coded *contemporaneous record* / *recollection* / *mixed*. **If recollection dominates after the record-first strategy has been taught, the strategy is not actionable as written** and the session should supply a worked search over a specific class of record.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of baseline records will omit the judge's model version from the pin, despite the pin being a required field and §3.5 being the material's longest subsection.
predictions.instrument: the submitted records, coded for pin completeness field by field. **This predicts the failure of §5's weakest countermeasure**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-3 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will produce disconfirming results judged capable of firing more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: a reviewer's binary judgement across two cohorts, or a within-cohort split on whether exercise 3 was completed. **This is the session's only direct test of the mechanism §3.13 rests on**, and a null result would mean the comparison requirement is ceremony.
